articles.title: Healey's Budget and the owner-managed manufacturer: exit relief, energy and jobs taxes
tldr: Healey is reported to be preparing to cut back Business Asset Disposal Relief, the tax break owners use when they sell.
Make UK wants electricity levies moved into general taxation and the employer NI threshold cut reversed.
Nothing is confirmed until Wednesday; the Treasury will not comment on speculation.
body: John Healey delivers his first Budget on Wednesday. For the owner of a small or mid-sized manufacturer, two questions matter most: what you will pay when you sell or retire, and what it will cost to run and staff a factory. Neither is settled yet, and the Treasury does not comment on speculation.

Start with selling up. The Telegraph reported last week that the Chancellor is preparing to scale back Business Asset Disposal Relief, the former entrepreneurs' relief, which lets owners pay a lower rate of capital gains tax on qualifying sales up to a lifetime limit of £1m. It has already been cut: Rachel Reeves raised the rate to 14%, and it rose again to 18% in April 2026. HMRC estimates the relief cost £800m in the latest tax year. The Treasury is reportedly weighing whether to use the savings for lower capital gains tax rates or for incentives aimed at founders who reinvest in new UK companies, an idea pushed by the Start Up Coalition and the Centre for British Progress. The Resolution Foundation, whose former chief executive Torsten Bell is now a Treasury minister, has called the relief "Britain's worst tax break".

The case against cutting it comes from the Federation of Small Businesses. Craig Beaumont said many owners fund their retirement through a sale, and the relief "must not be thoughtlessly discarded". Rathbones counted just under 5,800 business sales in 2025, the most in eight years. City AM reports that Healey has ruled out a rise in capital gains tax itself and has promised to back entrepreneurs who take risks, while founders lobby him to keep the relief.

This comes on top of the HMRC proposal, covered on Saturday, to tax share buy-backs used in family successions as income. An owner who planned to retire on a sale, or to hand the firm to the next generation, could face a higher bill either way.

Then running costs. Make UK's Budget submission asks Healey to move electricity policy levies into general taxation, to extend the British Industrial Competitiveness Scheme to all manufacturers and bring it forward, to reverse the cut in the employer National Insurance threshold, and to extend NI relief to all under-25s. It says Britain has Europe's highest industrial electricity prices, and that 56% of manufacturers think the country has become less attractive for investment over the past three to five years. The CBI wants the employer NI threshold raised from £5,000 to £6,000. Make UK's chief executive, Stephen Phipson, called the Budget "the first real test" of the government's plans to reindustrialise.

Its survey shows why. Spending on plant and machinery fell from 6.8% to 6.4% of turnover, and R&D from 6.2% to 5.1%. But 35% of manufacturers say a supportive tax regime would make them invest more, up from 24% last year.
On Wednesday, look for four things: any change to the relief's rate or £1m limit, the employer NI threshold, the treatment of energy levies, and whether reinvestment incentives for founders appear.
articles.why_it_matters: KHD is owner-managed, so any cut to Business Asset Disposal Relief bears directly on exit or retirement planning, and the employer NI threshold and industrial electricity levies affect the cost of hiring and running the workshop. Worth a word with the accountant before Wednesday about timing of any planned share transactions.

articles.title: Bird flu returns to a 32,000-hen free-range egg farm in Northumberland
tldr: H5N1 was confirmed on 19 October at a commercial free-range laying farm near Belford: about 32,000 hens will be culled.
It is the first H5N1 outbreak in British poultry this season, and Great Britain has lost its disease-free status for trade.
Egg producers' leaders say farm hygiene, fast culling and thorough cleansing and disinfection remain the main defence.
body: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) was confirmed on 19 October at a commercial free-range laying farm near Belford in north Northumberland. Farmers Weekly puts the flock at about 32,000 hens, all of which are to be culled. Defra has set up a 3km protection zone and a 10km surveillance zone around the premises.

Poultry Business describes it as the first confirmed H5N1 outbreak in poultry in Great Britain this season. It is the second highly pathogenic case overall: earlier in October an H5N5 strain was found in a small backyard flock at Ness on the Isle of Lewis. The commercial case has a wider consequence. Great Britain has lost its bird flu disease-free status, which affects international trade in poultry products.

The timing is no surprise to the industry. Migratory wild birds are arriving for the winter, and last season 100 premises were affected. Gary Ford, head of strategy at the British Free Range Egg Producers Association (BFREPA), called the case "not unexpected, but clearly disappointing for the industry". He said the control strategy has not changed: report early, cull fast, and clean and disinfect thoroughly. "The main approach to this dreadful disease is, as we know, farm hygiene," he told Farmers Weekly.

Ford also noted how culling has changed. About 60% of infected premises last season were whole-house gassed, and he expects similar practice this year. Will Raw, chair of the NFU Poultry Board, urged keepers of flocks of every size to keep biosecurity high and watch for signs of disease. The British Egg Industry Council has asked producers to keep the highest biosecurity standards and to record feed and water use accurately, so that health problems show up early.

There is some public money for prevention. Defra's Animal Health and Welfare Pathway, launched in May, pays for vet-led biosecurity reviews on poultry farms in England. Each review is worth £430, and eligible businesses can claim up to three visits per site. The vet assesses disease risks and writes up recommended improvements.

Vaccination is still not the answer for now. Trials continue, including recent work on turkeys, and Ford said "we believe it's effective, we believe it works". But trading partners would have to accept vaccinated birds and their products, and that remains the main obstacle.
For now the official risk to wild birds across Great Britain is rated medium, and the risk of poultry being exposed is rated low.
articles.why_it_matters: Every infected egg farm must be cleaned and disinfected before it restocks, and the BFREPA is again putting farm hygiene first. That is a natural opening for conversations with egg producers, packers and hatcheries in the north of England about hygiene equipment this winter. The £430 Defra biosecurity reviews may also produce written recommendations that steam cleaning can answer.

articles.title: Bimbo has spare bakery capacity and is hunting for the volume to fill it
tldr: The world's largest baker grew Q3 sales 3.6% and hit a record 15.7% margin, but North American volumes are still falling.
Its chief executive says the North American transformation is not finished until volume growth returns: "we have installed capacity".
US sandwich bread is shrinking in units, while specialty and crusty bread grow.
body: Grupo Bimbo reported its third-quarter results on 22 October. On paper they were strong. Group sales rose 3.6% excluding currency effects, adjusted EBITDA rose 9.3% and the margin reached a record 15.7%. The company raised its forecast for margin improvement this year to between 85 and 120 basis points.

North America is the problem. Sales there rose only 1% excluding currency, and price and product mix did all the work. Volumes fell. The regional margin improved by 40 basis points to 10.8%, the fifth quarter in a row of better margins, and Bimbo gained share in four of its six North American categories.

Chief executive Alejandro Rodríguez Bas was frank about it. "The transformation will not be completed until North America returns to sustained profitable volume growth," he said, and added: "The reality is we have installed capacity." In other words, Bimbo spent years adding lines and now needs to sell more bread through them.

The market is not helping. Circana data quoted by Bakery & Snacks for the 52 weeks to 9 August shows US centre-store sandwich bread sales down 1.5% in value and 3.3% in units. Nine of the ten biggest sellers sold fewer loaves. Private label grew 0.7% in value but its units fell 2.6%. The growth is in specialty bread, up 9% in value and 6% in units.

So Bimbo is looking for new customers. Greg Koehrsen, president of Bimbo Bakeries USA, said the business has always focused on large-format retail, and that smaller shops and food service are where it is less established.

Meanwhile it keeps squeezing costs. Commercial Baking lists the productivity programme: less waste, better recipes and packaging, more efficient plants, and leaner manufacturing footprints and delivery routes. Some capital projects have been pushed into 2027, and spending next year should be slightly above this year's. Bimbo has committed about $1bn (roughly £750m at summer 2026 exchange rates) to US investment in 2026 to 2028. Finance chief Diego Gaxiola warned that "2027 is going to be a challenge" because of costs, and the company expects more inflation from fuel, energy and raw materials.

The counter-argument is that margins are at a record and the volume loss is industry-wide, not Bimbo's alone. But a baker with idle capacity is more likely to invest in plant efficiency than in new lines.
articles.why_it_matters: Big bakers with spare capacity are spending on efficiency, waste and leaner plants rather than on new lines. Faster belt changeovers and less water, chemical and labour per clean fit that brief, so lead KHD pitches with cost per clean rather than added capacity. The same pressure on mass-market sandwich bread is likely in UK plant bakeries.

articles.title: Ipsos gives Labour its biggest lead of the parliament, with the Tories second and the Greens down
tldr: Ipsos: Labour 32, Conservatives 24, Reform 20, Lib Dems 9, Greens 8.
Opinium also has Labour eight points ahead, but with Reform second.
Four of the six latest polls put the Conservatives ahead of Reform.
body: Labour goes into the Budget with its best Ipsos poll of the parliament. The survey for LBC, carried out online between 15 and 22 October among 1,109 adults, puts Labour on 32%, up five points on September. The Conservatives are on 24% (up three), Reform UK 20% (down three), the Liberal Democrats 9% (up one) and the Greens 8% (down five).

Three things stand out. Labour's eight-point lead is the largest Ipsos has recorded this parliament. The Conservatives are in second place for the first time in the Ipsos series this parliament. And the Lib Dems have overtaken the Greens for fourth, after a five-point fall for Zack Polanski's party.

Other pollsters agree on the leader, not on second place. Opinium for The Observer, carried out from 21 to 23 October, has Labour on 30% (up one), Reform 22%, the Conservatives 20% (unchanged), the Greens 10% and the Lib Dems 9%. Its eight-point Labour lead is two points wider than in its previous poll. The Daily Britain's round-up of other recent polls lists Find Out Now at Labour 26, Conservatives 21, Reform 20; More in Common at 28, 23, 22; and YouGov at 27, 23, 22. Deltapoll has Labour 30, Reform 24, Conservatives 22. Four of the six latest polls put the Tories ahead of Reform; Opinium and Deltapoll do not.

Leader ratings move the same way. In the Ipsos poll, 35% are satisfied with Andy Burnham, up four, while 45% are dissatisfied. Kemi Badenoch is also on 35%, up seven and her best since becoming Leader of the Opposition. Nigel Farage fell to 22% and Polanski to 17%.

Ipsos's Keiran Pedley said Labour under Burnham is "resurgent, consolidating voters on the left behind them". The Greens' five-point slide fits that reading: Labour's gain appears to be coming mostly from voters on its left rather than directly from Reform. Pedley also warned that "we should be mindful against overreacting to one poll", and Ipsos noted that a tough Budget could throw Labour off course again.

The counter-argument is that the spread between pollsters is still wide. Labour's share runs from 26% to 32%, and whether Reform or the Conservatives are second depends on which firm you read. Wednesday's Budget, and the reaction to it in next week's polls, is the first real test of whether the Burnham bounce holds.

articles.title: Tories gain ground on Reform as voters doubt Farage's party is ready to govern
tldr: Only 19% now say Reform is ready to govern, down from 29% in September 2025; 24% say the same of the Tories.
The Conservatives are making defence their Budget attack line: fund 3% or resign.
Reform still owns immigration, at 28%, though that is down from 35% last November.
body: The contest on the right has shifted over the autumn, and the latest Ipsos poll puts numbers on it. Asked whether each party is ready to govern, 24% now say the Conservatives are, up four points on last month. Reform UK is at 19%, down from 29% in September 2025.

Personal ratings point the same way. Kemi Badenoch's satisfaction score is 35%, up seven points and her highest since she became Leader of the Opposition. Nigel Farage's has slipped to 22%. On issues, Reform still leads on asylum and immigration with 28%, against Labour's 14%, but that is down from a peak of 35% in November 2025. The Conservatives narrowly lead on defence, 19% to Labour's 18%, while Labour leads on the economy (20% to 18%) and the cost of living (21% to 13%).

The Conservatives are using the Budget to press that defence advantage. After the Sunday Times reported that Healey will announce billions of pounds of defence investment on Wednesday, the shadow chancellor, Andrew Griffith, said: "By the end of his Budget statement, John Healey must have fully funded three per cent defence spending, or resign." The demand is pointed because Healey quit as defence secretary in June over the same target. The shadow defence secretary, James Cartlidge, welcomed the investment with "I welcome Labour copying our idea", but said technology money was no substitute for training, equipment and ammunition. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates that reaching 3% of GDP would need an extra £17.3bn in 2029-30.

Labour's reply came from the defence secretary, Wes Streeting, who said Badenoch's party had "shrunk the British Army to its smallest size since the Napoleonic era" and left a £17bn hole in the equipment plan.
The Tory message to right-leaning voters is blunt: a Conservative spokesman said "a vote for any party other than the Conservatives risks condemning the country to a future under Labour."

Across the wider field, four of the six latest voting-intention polls now put the Conservatives ahead of Reform, according to a round-up by The Daily Britain. That is a reversal of the position for much of the past year, when Reform was regularly ahead of both main parties.

The counter-argument: Opinium and Deltapoll still put Reform second, Ipsos itself warns against reading too much into one poll, and Reform's lead on immigration, the issue that built its support, remains large.

articles.title: Healey to route defence billions through the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank
tldr: The Sunday Times says the Budget will put billions into UK defence firms via the two state-backed lenders, funded by borrowing.
Drone makers and AI companies are expected to benefit; the Treasury is said to be preparing £20.4bn more for the two bodies from 2028-29.
The 3% of GDP target is not expected to be met in this Budget.
body: John Healey is expected to use Wednesday's Budget to announce billions of pounds of new defence investment, according to the Sunday Times. The money is not expected to come through the Ministry of Defence's own budget. Instead, City AM reports, it will be channelled through the National Wealth Fund and the British Business Bank to UK defence manufacturers and military technology firms, with drone makers and AI companies among those expected to benefit.

The method matters as much as the sum. The Sunday Times says the investment will be paid for with long-term borrowing rather than spending cuts. Because lending through these public financial institutions is expected to earn a return, it is treated differently from ordinary spending under the fiscal rules. That lets the Treasury put more into defence without breaching its rules, and the money would still count towards NATO spending targets. The Treasury is reported to be preparing £20.4bn of extra support for the two bodies from 2028-29, although how much of it will go to defence has not been confirmed.

No headline figure for defence has been given. UK Fact Check, which logged the Sunday Times report, notes that PA has reported Healey's promise to fill a £4.7bn "black hole" in the Defence Investment Plan, and that the Sunday Times does not say whether the new money would cover that gap. The Treasury has not confirmed the report.

The 3% target is the sore point. Healey resigned as defence secretary in June, arguing that the plan fell short and calling for a timetable to reach 3% of GDP by 2030. As Chancellor, he has said a full timetable will wait until next year's spending review, and PA reports that the 3% aim is not expected to be met in this Budget. The Office for Budget Responsibility estimates 3% would need an extra £17.3bn in 2029-30.

For manufacturers outside defence, what matters is the method of funding rather than the sum. Using the National Wealth Fund and British Business Bank as investors lets a Chancellor with little headroom back favoured sectors without the money showing up as day-to-day spending.

The counter-argument is that investment returns are not guaranteed and borrowing is still borrowing. Shadow defence secretary James Cartlidge said technology investment is no substitute for funding training, equipment and ammunition.

articles.title: Storm Shadows and drones hit Russian titanium and missile-battery plants
tldr: Drones struck the Avisma titanium plant in Berezniki, about 1,500km from Ukraine, on 25 October
Storm Shadow cruise missiles reportedly hit the Energiya plant in Yelets, which makes batteries for Iskander, Kinzhal and glide bombs
Russia admits damage at both sites but says the titanium plant kept working
body: Ukraine spent Sunday hitting two links in Russia's weapons supply chain at opposite ends of its range. One target was the Avisma titanium works in Berezniki in the Urals. The other was the Energiya power-source plant at Yelets in Lipetsk region, much closer to the border. Kyiv has not formally claimed either strike; the targets were identified by the Ukrainian monitoring channel Exilenova+ and other open-source analysts, and Russian governors confirmed attacks on unnamed industrial sites.

Avisma, part of VSMPO-Avisma, is one of the world's largest producers of titanium sponge and Russia's biggest titanium producer. Its metal goes into military aircraft and their engines, missiles, nuclear submarines, armoured vehicles and space hardware, and it has been under US sanctions since 2023. Berezniki lies about 170km north of Perm; the Kyiv Independent puts it more than 1,400km from the Ukrainian border and Euromaidan Press about 1,500km. Perm's governor, Dmitry Makhonin, said 11 drones were downed around 11am local time, that a facility in the north of the region suffered "minor" damage and kept operating, and that five employees were hurt. Neither outlet identifies the drone type used.

Yelets is about 250km from the border, and the weapon there was reportedly different. Exilenova+ said the plant was struck with Storm Shadow cruise missiles, the British-supplied air-launched weapon, and the Dnipro OSINT channel said at least two missiles hit two buildings. Energiya is described as Russia's largest maker of electrochemical power sources. According to Dnipro OSINT, its batteries go into Iskander-K and Iskander-M missiles, the Kh-47M2 Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missile, Zircon, the Pantsir air-defence system and UMPB D-30SN guided bombs. Exilenova+ calls it Russia's only producer of batteries for the planning and correction modules that turn old bombs into glide bombs. It also makes drone batteries. The plant has been hit before, in May and July 2025 and January 2026. Lipetsk's governor, Igor Artamonov, said an "industrial zone" was targeted and one person was injured.

The pattern is deliberate. Two days earlier Storm Shadows were reported to have hit the Proton-Electrotex electronics plant in Oryol, which Ukraine's General Staff says makes components for Iskander-M and S-71 cruise missiles; the Oryol governor said three bodies were found in the rubble. The same weekend monitoring channels reported a fire at the Omsky Kauchuk petrochemical plant in Omsk, about 2,500km from Ukraine.

The caution: none of the damage has been independently assessed, and Moscow says Avisma is working normally. Plants making components can often be repaired or their output spread elsewhere, so the real test is whether Russian missile and glide-bomb use drops in the weeks ahead.

articles.title: Zelensky offers an energy truce and sets his terms for November's three-way talks
tldr: Ukraine will stop hitting Russian refineries if Russia stops hitting its power grid, Zelensky says
He wants technical talks on energy, grain and prisoners first; territory only at leader level
Moscow says talks can resume only after its 4 November holiday
body: Volodymyr Zelensky has set out what Ukraine will bring to the three-way talks with American and Russian negotiators expected in the first half of November, and put a concrete offer on the table: a mutual halt to strikes on energy. "If you want us to stop striking Russia's diesel and oil refining infrastructure, it's very simple," he told Alla Mazur of the TSN programme on Sunday evening. "An energy ceasefire. That's how it can work." He said he had put the idea to Ukraine's partners and described the refinery campaign as a response to Russian attacks on Ukraine's grid, "a matter of fairness".

His proposed agenda is narrow. "Energy, grain, and people – these are the specifics," he said: an energy ceasefire, a new arrangement to protect grain shipping in the Black Sea, and prisoner exchanges. He stressed these were proposals to Washington rather than demands, and that a Russian refusal to discuss them would show whether the Kremlin was serious. He suggested Vladimir Putin might be agreeing to talk only to avoid friction with Washington before the US midterms on 3 November: "We will very quickly see in November whether it was a trick or not."

On sequencing, he wants technical teams to meet before any meeting of himself, Putin and Donald Trump. Territory is a "red line" that only leaders can discuss, and "we are not exchanging anything for anything". Security guarantees "cannot be dictated by the Russian side", he said, and limits on Ukraine's army or neutrality are "not up for discussion". If NATO membership is blocked he wants the US and European countries to extend Article 5-style protection, and he would like to keep an army of 800,000 if it can be paid for, fewer if Ukraine joins NATO.

He also warned that easing sanctions before the talks would weaken Ukraine's hand, a pointed reference to Mr Trump's waiver on Russian oil exports earlier this month. After meeting the US envoy Steve Witkoff in Oslo, he said disputes over Starlink and US intelligence sharing were settled for now, but air defence shortages remained: "There is progress; it's just very slow."

Moscow's timetable is looser. Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov said on Sunday that "the next deadline is now Nov. 4, our major holiday" and that Russia would be ready to resume talks after that. The strongest case against Kyiv's approach is that it has little leverage: Mr Trump has told Mr Zelensky he has "very few cards", and an energy truce would also spare Russian refineries that Ukraine's drones have been hitting hard.

articles.title: Named Russian war dead pass 280,000 in independent count
tldr: Mediazona and BBC Russian have identified 282,993 Russian military dead by name
6,880 names were added in under three weeks; 7,920 officers and 15 generals are confirmed
The journalists say the true toll is likely significantly higher
body: The independent Russian outlet Mediazona, working with the BBC's Russian service, has now confirmed the names of 282,993 Russian military personnel killed in Ukraine between the full-scale invasion on 24 February 2022 and 23 October 2026. The latest update added 6,880 names since the previous count in early October.

The figure is a floor, not an estimate. Each name has to be backed by an obituary, an official or media report, a verifiable post by relatives, or evidence such as photographs or funeral dates. Deaths that are never made public are missed, recent months are the least complete, and fighters of the Donetsk and Luhansk proxy forces are excluded unless they held Russian citizenship. The journalists say the real number is "likely significantly higher". Mediazona keeps a separate statistical estimate based on probate records and excess male mortality, but that was last updated in May with data to the end of 2025.

The list also shows how Russia is fighting. It contains 7,920 officers of the army and other security agencies and 15 generals. The officers' share of deaths fell from as much as 10% early in the war to 2–3% by November 2024, which Mediazona attributes to Russia's growing reliance on contract volunteers recruited for infantry assaults, who are far more likely to die. By September 2024 volunteers were again the largest category of the dead; convicts recruited from prisons dominated in early 2023 around Bakhmut, and have not been used en masse since. In the war's first six months, men aged 21 to 23 died in the largest numbers; volunteers now are generally over 30.

Other counts are larger because they measure something different. Ukraine's General Staff says Russia has lost 1,578,450 troops, a figure for killed and wounded together. The Center for Strategic and International Studies in Washington estimated in July about 1.4 million Russian casualties, against 525,000 to 625,000 for Ukraine. None of these can be checked independently, and Moscow publishes no figures.

articles.title: The MoD puts up to £2bn on replacing the SA80 rifle, and asks small firms to talk
tldr: A new MoD notice values Project GRAYBURN, the SA80 replacement, at up to £2bn including VAT, with a contract running from July 2029 to March 2045.
The rifle must be made in the UK and beat modern body armour; the calibre is still undecided.
An invitation-only industry day is open to registrations until 5pm on 30 October, and the notice says it suits SMEs.
body: The Ministry of Defence has put a price on replacing the British Army's rifle for the first time. A notice issued on 23 October by the National Armaments Director Group values Project GRAYBURN at £2bn including VAT (about £1.67bn without), according to the UK Defence Journal. The contract is expected to run from July 2029 to the end of March 2045. A January pipeline notice had given 2028 to 2045 and no value at all; in April 2025 the then minister Maria Eagle told Parliament the project was too early for a cost estimate.

GRAYBURN replaces the whole SA80 family, in service since the 1980s and rebuilt twice: the A2 by Heckler & Koch and the current A3 with a new upper receiver. The January notice set out five variants, likely on a common lower receiver: a standard close-combat rifle to replace the L85A3, a shorter close-combat version, a personal defence weapon to replace the L22 carbine, a 'generalist' rifle to replace the L85A2, and a cadet rifle to replace the L98. Janes has reported a buy of about 170,000 weapons.

The requirements are specific. The rifle must defeat current and emerging enemy body armour, carry day optics as standard and take in-line night sights quickly, reduce its signature on some variants, and work in every climate. It must be made in the UK, and the MoD wants a possible long-term 'strategic supplier' that would deliver, support and keep developing the weapon. The calibre is open: performance, compatibility with allies and complexity are all being weighed. The notice says no procurement route, supplier, product or contract structure has been chosen.

For firms, the near-term detail is the industry day. It is hybrid and by invitation, each organisation gets one 15-minute one-to-one, registration closes at 5pm on 30 October and the engagement deadline is 27 November. The MoD says the sessions will not be used to evaluate or down-select suppliers and describes the opportunity as particularly suitable for small and medium-sized enterprises. The formal tender is not expected until 2 July 2027.

Some bidders are already positioning. Janes reported last November that Beretta Defense Technologies is offering its NARP and Sako ARG rifles with Norma ammunition and Steiner optics, and has drawn up a plan to turn an existing Lincolnshire site into a small-arms production hub with up to 70 skilled jobs, with options from 5% to 100% UK manufacture.

The catch is timing and money. The L85A3's out-of-service date has already slipped from 2030 into the early 2030s, so soldiers will carry the old rifle while the new one is delivered. A senior official said in July that GRAYBURN 'is funded', yet it has no specific line in the Defence Investment Plan.

articles.title: Denmark picks a two-year-old start-up's cruise missile for its first long-range strike weapon
tldr: Denmark will buy Kongsberg's air-launched Joint Strike Missile and the ground-launched Anthem cruise missile from the US-Israeli start-up Covenant.

body: Denmark has chosen a start-up's missile to give it a long-range strike capability for the first time. Defence minister Jeppe Bruus said on 22 October that the country will buy two weapons: Kongsberg's Joint Strike Missile, which its F-35s can carry, and a ground-launched cruise missile called Anthem from Covenant, a young US-based company, Defense News reported. Bruus called it 'a significant step toward improving Denmark's self-defence capabilities'. The purpose is to be able to hit back at an attacker, and Denmark has promised NATO such a capability by 2030. Officials gave no quantities, costs or delivery dates.

Covenant is about two years old, with roots in Israel and the US, founded by Michael Kaufman and Ofir Dayan. In early October it opened a site of about 10,000 square metres in north Leipzig, its third after Israel and Dallas, which Defence Network reports as a €250m investment (a little over £200m). According to Danish broadcaster TV2, Denmark's missiles will be made there.

What is known about Anthem is thin, and much of it comes from the company. Covenant has not published a range; observers estimate up to 1,500km, between Taurus (over 500km) and Tomahawk (up to 2,000km). Observers put the warhead at 200 to 300kg, roughly half what those two can carry in some versions. It first flew in August 2025 and Covenant says it has run more than 200 tests, including flights with the US military. It is sold as a complete package covering transport, storage and ground launch, with mission-planning software for coordinated mass launches.

The pitch is price and volume. Covenant says Anthem will cost a 'mid six-figure' sum per missile in serial production (it does not give a currency), against more than a million for Taurus or Tomahawk. It plans 1,000 missiles in 2027, its first year of production, and up to 5,000 a year after that, and says fewer than 5% of components in the German-built version will come from outside Europe.

That is why Berlin is watching. Germany plans to spend €12bn (about £10bn) closing its deep-strike gap: buying about 400 Tomahawks from the US, developing a missile with Britain over the longer term, and in the meantime looking at cheap, high-volume options including Anthem and two Ukrainian systems. Its defence ministry has confirmed only that it is in talks with Covenant.

The counter-argument is plain: Anthem has never been fired in anger, and every production target depends on a factory that has not yet built a missile. For a start-up, though, a NATO government order before serial production begins is a large vote of confidence.

articles.title: Kremlin says a Putin–Xi–Trump summit in Shenzhen is being prepared, but Beijing has not said so
tldr: Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov says Moscow, Beijing and Washington are 'in principle ready' for a three-way summit at APEC in Shenzhen on 18–19 November.
Trump says he would go to talk about nuclear weapons, 'not so much for Ukraine'; China's foreign ministry has said only that it has no information.
Kyiv and European voices warn of a great-power deal over Ukraine's head.
body: The Kremlin says work has begun on the first summit between the leaders of Russia, China and the United States. Yuri Ushakov, Vladimir Putin's foreign policy aide, told Russian state television on Sunday that "Moscow, Beijing and Washington are in principle ready to hold it, and preparations have already begun." The meeting would take place on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders' summit in Shenzhen, China, on 18–19 November.

Ushakov said Russia and America had not yet agreed a separate Putin–Trump meeting in Shenzhen, "because so far we have been talking about this trilateral contact", though he said one was possible. He tied Putin's attendance at the G20 summit in Miami in December, for which the Kremlin has received a formal invitation, to how Shenzhen goes: "first comes November, and then comes December." He also said Russia would be ready to resume talks in the Russia–US–Ukraine format after its National Unity Day on 4 November, describing the planned expert-level meeting as "exploratory".

Donald Trump first said he was open to the idea on 19 October. He said he would go "not so much for Ukraine" but "to talk about nuclear weapons and denuclearisation", while adding that he would do "whatever I can do to end the war." The Wall Street Journal has reported that Moscow wants to use such a meeting to settle the war on terms favourable to Russia, according to reports relaying its story.

Beijing has been far more guarded. When asked about a three-way meeting on 19 October, foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said she had no information to share, and none of the reports read here carries a Chinese confirmation of Ushakov's claim. Even the Kremlin has been less certain at times: Dmitry Peskov said last week that "no substantive proposals or agreements" on the meeting or its agenda had been put forward.

For Xi, hosting such a meeting would put China at the centre of the table with both nuclear superpowers, on home ground. For Europe and Ukraine the format is the worry. Ukraine's foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, said a three-way meeting of the Russian, Chinese and American leaders "would do only the opposite" of helping peace, and former prime minister Arseniy Yatsenyuk compared such arrangements to Munich in 1938 and Yalta in 1945. Volodymyr Zelensky has insisted no deal on Ukraine's borders can be made "over Kyiv's head".

The counter-argument is that the summit may never happen in this form: so far it rests on Russian statements, and both Washington and Beijing have stopped short of committing to it. The next signal to watch is whether China's foreign ministry says anything once the party plenum ends on Thursday.

articles.title: China's stock market slides into a bear market as company profits disappoint
tldr: The blue-chip CSI 300 is more than 20% below its June peak and was heading for an 11th straight weekly fall, the longest run since the index began in 2005.
Chinese shares have lost about $3.5 trillion (roughly £2.6 trillion) since May, and reported profits are missing forecasts by an average of 9%.
Beijing is propping prices up through state funds but is avoiding a big stimulus, and the party plenum that opens today is about discipline, not the economy.
body: China's stock market has crossed into bear territory. The blue-chip CSI 300 index is more than 20% below its closing peak of 22 June, Reuters reported, and on Friday it was on course for an 11th consecutive weekly fall, the longest losing run since the index was created in 2005. On Thursday it posted its lowest close since July 2025, and the Shanghai Composite ended at its weakest level in more than a year. On Friday morning tech shares took the worst of it: Shanghai's STAR50 index fell 3.1% and the ChiNext start-up board 2.1%.

Bloomberg puts the loss in market value since a peak in May at $3.5 trillion, roughly £2.6 trillion at about 75p to the dollar. Its central point is that this is now about earnings, not just mood. Consensus 2026 profit forecasts for members of the MSCI China index have fallen by more than 4% since the end of March, and by more than 13% for the Hang Seng Tech index. Companies that have reported so far have missed forecasts by an average of 9%, the second-worst quarterly miss in two years. China Mobile's profit for January to September fell 8%; the battery maker CATL and Ganfeng Lithium also missed. Alibaba's sale of $10 billion (about £7.5 billion) of new shares has diluted existing holders.

The underlying problem is price wars and weak consumer demand, which turn sales growth into thinner margins. "Competition is encouraged and generally brutal in China, not shareholder friendly," said Jason Lemire of Bold Wealth Partners. A sell-off in American tech on Thursday, after earnings raised fears about AI spending, added pressure on Chinese AI hardware stocks.

Beijing's response has been to steady prices rather than to boost demand. Trading spiked on Friday in exchange-traded funds favoured by the state-backed "national team", which eased the losses. But policymakers have preferred small, incremental measures to the large packages of 2024, and RBC Wealth Management blamed the slump on "insufficient fiscal stimulus and disappointing earnings", warning that without new policy or technology catalysts "volatile trading may persist into early 2027." Third-quarter growth of 4.5% has put the year back within the government's 4.5–5% target, which reduces the pressure to act. As William Bratton of BNP Paribas put it, "Policymakers are comfortable with the nature of economic growth."
The four-day party plenum that opens in Beijing today is not expected to change that: last year's plenum set the five-year economic plan, and this one is focused on party discipline.

The counter-argument: some investors think the sell-off has gone far enough. Bridgewater's China arm has turned "prudently optimistic", arguing that third-quarter falls were driven mainly by liquidity rather than valuations. Berenberg's Ulrich Urbahn is not convinced: "It is too early to conclude that the worst is over."

articles.title: US banks shut the door on AI agents that log in with customers' passwords
tldr: JPMorgan, Citi, Bank of America and Schwab say they are blocking or restricting outside AI agents that log into customer accounts.
The problem is customers handing usernames and passwords to personal AI assistants the banks have never vetted.
Read-only access through open-banking providers is the route banks still allow; anything that moves money needs a human.
body: America's biggest banks are pushing back against a new kind of customer: the personal AI agent. Axios reported on 22 October that banks are detecting activity from third-party agents inside customers' online accounts, an industrywide problem touching dozens of institutions, according to Axios's Madison Mills. CBS News, following up the next day, said the agents were not hacking accounts or draining them. They were mostly doing what their users told them, using usernames and passwords the users had handed over.

That is the sticking point. Sharing login details breaks the banks' terms of service, and some agents have taken steps their owners never approved, such as contacting a bank with a complaint without asking the account holder first. Meta's Muse assistant, launched in September, sharpened the worry: FStech reports that banks fear agents will start moving idle cash into higher-interest accounts on their owners' behalf.

The banks have responded one by one. Jamie Dimon told JPMorgan's 13 October earnings call that the bank would not let "just any outside agents" into its systems, and warned there could be thousands of rogue ones. Citi said it will not allow third-party AI agents or assistants to log into a customer's account or transact on its platforms. Schwab's chief executive, Rick Wurster, said it is blocking unauthorised agents. Bank of America's Brian Moynihan said it is restricting access while it works out who is liable when an AI authorises a payment, telling CNBC there should be "a human in the loop" before money leaves an account.

There is also a money motive. A report cited by FStech says JPMorgan, Bank of America and Wells Fargo hold $1.6 trillion (about £1.2 trillion, converted at roughly $1.34 to the pound) in deposits that pay no interest, 16% of their liabilities. Paying 3% on that would cost them $47 billion a year (about £35 billion), nearly half their combined earnings. Agents that shop around for yield threaten that cheap funding.

The counter-argument came from David Sacks, the White House AI adviser, who wrote that agents acting with their owner's permission are "in no way cyberattacks" and should not be lumped in with rogue ones. He suggested banks offer read-only access, letting an agent see activity but not act on it, while treating full access with user credentials carefully.

That is where the practical line is settling. Citi still lets customers give limited, read-only access through certain open-banking providers, and Chase says it supports customer-authorised data sharing through such providers rather than shared passwords. For a small firm trying an AI assistant on its books, the lesson is the same on either side of the Atlantic: connect it through the bank's approved data feed, keep it read-only, and keep payments in human hands. Giving it your banking password risks breaching your bank's terms and leaves the question of who pays for a mistake unanswered.

body: Two industrial software firms announced AI products for the factory floor on 22 October. Rockwell Automation added support for NVIDIA's open Nemotron models to FactoryTalk Conductor, its recently introduced platform that lets engineers start automation tasks in plain language and hands them to Rockwell-verified AI agents. The point of the open models, Rockwell says, is that customers can keep engineering and production data in their own environments and control cost and governance. Engineers stay responsible for checking and approving the work. Commercial availability is expected in the first quarter of 2027.

L2L, a Salt Lake City maker of plant operations software, launched Shop Floor Execution, which is available now. Its "Execution AI" offers voice-driven dispatching of maintenance jobs, automatic logging of line events, and troubleshooting that suggests a fix by searching how similar faults were resolved before. L2L claims return on investment in as little as four weeks.

Both are vendor announcements with no named users or measured results, and both are aimed at large plants. The idea a small manufacturer can copy today is cheaper: write every breakdown and its fix into a searchable log. That record is what L2L's troubleshooting feature runs on, and it is useful to an engineer or a general-purpose AI assistant long before any new platform is bought.

articles.title: The gallium neutrino anomaly may be a calculation error, not new physics
tldr: For 30 years gallium detectors have caught about 20% fewer neutrinos from radioactive sources than predicted, now a gap of more than 5 sigma.
The favourite explanation, a sterile neutrino, clashes with reactor and solar data.
An Italian team says the standard cross-section calculation wrongly separates the electron from the nuclear transition; doing it properly lowers the prediction enough to close the gap.
body: The gallium anomaly is one of neutrino physics' stubborn loose ends. In the GALLEX, SAGE and BEST experiments, intense radioactive sources of chromium-51 or argon-37, which emit electron neutrinos of fixed energy, were placed inside large volumes of gallium. A neutrino can turn a gallium-71 nucleus into germanium-71 and an electron, a charged-current weak process in which a neutron becomes a proton. Counting the germanium atoms gives the capture rate. The count has come out about 20% low for three decades, and with BEST's 2022 result the discrepancy now exceeds 5 sigma.

The popular reading has been oscillation into a sterile neutrino, a hypothetical state that does not feel the weak force. The trouble is that the oscillation parameters it needs sit badly with reactor antineutrino experiments, solar neutrino bounds and neutrino mass measurements.

A paper in Physical Review Letters, published on 24 September and written up by Phys.org on 16 October, attacks the prediction instead. Matteo Cadeddu of Italy's INFN and colleagues, including Carlo Giunti, who first set out the anomaly clearly in 2007, question how the capture cross-section is computed. The standard method fixes its size from the measured half-life of germanium-71, which decays back to gallium-71 by electron capture, using detailed balance. In doing so it factorises the problem: the lepton wave functions are treated as a simple factor, separate from a single nuclear matrix element for the Gamow-Teller transition.

The authors drop that factorisation. They use relativistic electron wave functions from the Dirac equation and Gamow-Teller transition densities that keep track of where in the nucleus the transition happens, constrained to reproduce the germanium half-life. Relativistic wave functions alone did not fix things, Cadeddu told Phys.org; the point is that "the electron and the nuclear transition cannot always be treated as two essentially independent pieces". The revised cross-section is significantly smaller. The paper's abstract says this could resolve the anomaly without new physics; Phys.org reports the predicted capture rate now matches what was observed.

The caution is that the answer now leans on nuclear-structure inputs, and no other group has yet reproduced it. If it holds, it removes one of the main experimental hints for sterile neutrinos. It is also a reminder that an anomaly can sit in a textbook approximation as easily as in the Standard Model.

articles.title: A proof that no quantum process thermalises in less than ħ/2k_BT
tldr: Physicists in Vienna, Barcelona and Geneva have proved a universal lower limit on how fast any quantum process can bring a system to thermal equilibrium.
Above the gap scale the limit is half the 'Planckian time' ħ/k_BT; near zero temperature it becomes ħ/Δ, set by the energy gap.
The proof comes from quantum estimation theory: a faster thermaliser would beat the Heisenberg limit.
body: The 'Planckian time', ħ/k_BT, keeps turning up in condensed-matter physics. Strange metals with resistivity linear in temperature appear to scatter electrons at about this rate, and Maldacena, Shenker and Stanford's bound on quantum chaos has the same form. It has long been suspected to be a speed limit for thermal processes, but without a general proof. A paper in Nature Physics, reported by Phys.org on 18 October, supplies one for thermalisation.

The authors, Paolo Abiuso (IQOQI Vienna, Austrian Academy of Sciences), Alberto Rolandi (TU Wien), John Calsamiglia (Universitat Autònoma de Barcelona), Pavel Sekatski (Geneva) and Martí Perarnau-Llobet (Barcelona and Geneva), set the problem up very generally. A 'thermalisation machine' of any size, coupled to the system as strongly as you like and evolving under the Schrödinger equation, must take the system to within a small error of its Gibbs state at temperature T. Crucially, it must do this not for one Hamiltonian but for a set of nearby ones.

The argument is then one of distinguishability. If two slightly different Hamiltonians are each driven to their own thermal state, the outputs are distinguishable by a known amount. But the dynamics can only make them distinguishable so fast: the quantum Fisher information gained from evolving for time τ grows at most as τ²/ħ² times the squared norm of the perturbing operator, the generalised Heisenberg limit. As the authors put it, "the thermalization machine cannot violate the Heisenberg limit". Matching the two gives τ ≥ ħ/(2k_BT) when k_BT is comparable to or above the spectral gap Δ, and τ ≥ ħ/Δ at low temperature, which they link to the quantum adiabatic theorem.

Plugging in numbers: ħ/k_B is about 7.6 picosecond-kelvins, so at room temperature, 300 K, the floor is roughly 13 femtoseconds; at 1 K it is about 3.8 picoseconds. Pumping in more energy or driving harder cannot beat it.

The requirement to work for a family of Hamiltonians matters. For a single known Hamiltonian, a machine that simply swaps in a prepared Gibbs state can act almost instantly, so no bound applies. The authors show the bound can be tight in a fine-tuned two-Hamiltonian case and a fermionic resonant-level model, but leave open how close realistic many-body systems come to it and how entanglement and system size change the picture. The work was first posted on arXiv in June 2025.

briefs.summary: Russia launched 153 Shahed-type drones at Ukraine overnight on 25 October, 92 of them jet-powered, plus low-cost Banderol cruise missiles. Ukraine downed 119, including 64 jet drones. Attacks over the day killed 8 people and injured 51; a drone hit a five-storey block of flats in Vinnytsia, destroying four apartments.

sources.title: Russian attacks kill 8, injure 51 across Ukraine over past day as drone strikes residential building in Vinnytsia

briefs.title: Trump says the US will do business with both Russia and Ukraine after the war
briefs.summary: Donald Trump said on 24 October he expects America to "do business with Ukraine and with Russia after this war ends". The remarks came as the first tanker of Russian diesel, 40,000 tonnes, sailed from Primorsk for New York under a deal European allies, Kyiv and members of Congress say undermines sanctions. Around 900,000 tonnes are planned.

sources.title: Trump wants 'business with both' Ukraine, Russia after war ends

briefs.title: Lula, a would-be Ukraine peace mediator, wins a fourth term in Brazil
briefs.summary: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva beat Flávio Bolsonaro 51.79% to 48.21% in Brazil's run-off on 25 October; Bolsonaro refuses to concede. Lula has pitched Brazil as a mediator between Kyiv and Moscow, meeting Zelensky at the G7 in June and speaking to Putin in August, while staying out of Western sanctions on Russia.

sources.title: Bolsonaro refuses to concede as would-be Ukraine peace mediator Lula wins Brazil election

briefs.title: Ukraine's General Staff confirms hits on Tolyatti rubber plant and an aircraft at Yeysk
briefs.summary: Ukraine's General Staff said on 24 October its forces struck the Tolyattikauchuk synthetic rubber plant in Tolyatti, Samara region, and an aircraft at Yeysk airfield. Drone attacks the previous day forced flight restrictions at Moscow's Sheremetyevo, Domodedovo, Vnukovo and Zhukovsky airports.

briefs.title: Ukrainian drone attack hits shopping centre in Belgorod
briefs.summary: An overnight Ukrainian drone attack on Belgorod on 25 October damaged a shopping and entertainment centre, residential buildings and cars, according to the monitoring channel Exilenova+. Belgorod's mayor, Valentin Demidov, said one person was killed and ten injured. Ukraine's General Staff said it hit Russian military radar stations in the region the same night.

briefs.title: Russia claims it downed 532 Ukrainian drones in one night
briefs.summary: Russia's defence ministry said via TASS that its air defences destroyed 532 Ukrainian drones overnight into 25 October over 23 regions and the Sea of Azov, including over Perm region and around Moscow. The figure has not been independently verified. Strikes that night included the Avisma titanium plant in Berezniki and the Energiya battery plant in Yelets.

sources.title: Russian titanium plant in Urals reportedly hit by Ukrainian drones, 1,500 km from Ukraine

briefs.title: Oleshky evacuation ceasefire set for 27 October, but Zelensky doubts Russia will let people go
briefs.summary: A local ceasefire to evacuate the occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson region is planned for 27 October. Zelensky said it would need to last several days and require Russian help, and that Moscow is unlikely to let residents leave freely; some may be evacuated to Ukrainian-held areas. A former resident warned people "won't survive this winter".

briefs.title: Lib Dems propose three more Type 26 and three more Type 31 frigates
briefs.summary: The Liberal Democrats want six more frigates ordered next Parliament for delivery by the mid-2030s, taking Type 26 numbers from 8 to 11 and Type 31 from 5 to 8. They cost it at about £4.42bn of capital, including £370m for two new shipbuilding facilities, paid for by raising the Digital Services Tax from 2% to 10%.

sources.title: Lib Dems propose six more frigates for Royal Navy

briefs.title: £290m set aside to replace the Army's Point-class sealift ships
briefs.summary: The Defence Investment Plan allocates £290m for a future strategic sealift capability; the current Foreland Shipping contract for four privately owned Point-class ro-ro ships ends on 31 December 2031. A January request to industry asked for up to six ships and 15,600 lane metres in a crisis, about 60% more than today, able to carry the heavier Challenger 3.

sources.title: Sealift replacement gets two hundred and ninety million

briefs.title: No service dates yet for the Royal Navy's drone warships
briefs.summary: Defence minister Luke Pollard told MPs no in-service dates have been set for the Common Combat Vessel or the four uncrewed types of the 'Hybrid Navy' (Type 91 missile platform, Type 92 underwater sensor, Type 93 extra-large underwater vessel, Type 94 radar platform). Planning assumes they arrive progressively from the early 2030s; the Defence Investment Plan gives at least £1.3bn.

sources.title: No service dates set for Royal Navy's drone warships

briefs.title: DragonFire laser stays a sovereign programme, with no role for Ukraine for now
briefs.summary: Asked whether Ukraine could join the DragonFire laser weapon programme, Luke Pollard said the MoD is focused on 'maturing advanced sovereign technologies' and gave no commitment. DragonFire, built by MBDA, Leonardo and QinetiQ with Dstl, is being accelerated onto a Type 45 destroyer, with its in-service date brought forward from 2032 to the late 2020s.

sources.title: DragonFire stays a sovereign programme for now

briefs.title: £2.45m UK-Australian competition seeks better battlefield power for soldiers
briefs.summary: UK Defence Innovation, for the British Army and with Australia's ASCA accelerator, has opened the £2.45m Tactical Power Challenge for new ways to generate, store, distribute and manage power for deployed troops. Bids close at noon on 10 November. Radios, EW detectors, night vision and counter-drone kit are making battery weight and generator signatures a real constraint.

sources.title: Army seeks new ways to power troops on the battlefield

briefs.title: Three in four defence tech firms say the UK market has shrunk, techUK tells MPs
briefs.summary: techUK told the Defence Committee that 73% of its defence tech members say the market has declined and 93% are rethinking investment or hiring. Chief executive Julian David said MoD commercial teams run at 70% headcount, 40% of them contractors, and only £2bn of the £7.5bn SME target is direct spend. The FSB said 19% of small firms that dealt with the MoD would not again.

sources.title: Most defence tech firms report a declining market

briefs.title: £470m for base security after intruders at RAF Molesworth and Fairford
briefs.summary: Two Latvian nationals were arrested inside RAF Molesworth, which hosts US and NATO intelligence work, earlier in October, and there was a separate incident at RAF Fairford. Armed forces minister Louise Sandher-Jones said £470m over four years will go on site protection, surveillance, counter-drone kit and wider restricted airspace around defence sites.

sources.title: Base security boosted after Fairford and Molesworth breaches

briefs.title: Seven Challenger 3 prototypes delivered for trials
briefs.summary: RBSL in Telford has delivered seven of eight Challenger 3 prototypes for firing, mobility, electromagnetic and safety trials before the MoD commits to building the rest of the 148 tanks. The tank pairs a Challenger 2 hull with a new turret, smoothbore NATO-standard gun, modular armour and active protection; initial operating capability is planned for 2027 and full capability for 2030.

sources.title: Seven Challenger 3 tank prototypes delivered for trials

briefs.title: Xi's party plenum opens in Beijing with attendance expected at a record low
briefs.summary: The Communist Party's four-day fifth plenum opened on Monday and runs to Thursday, focused on a decision on 'comprehensively and strictly governing the party'. The Asia Society Policy Institute projects only 291 of 376 Central Committee members will attend (77%), below the previous low of 315 at last year's plenum, as purges thin the ranks a year before Xi's expected bid for a fourth term.

briefs.title: Kim Jong-un crosses the new Yalu bridge into China on his first known trip abroad in a year
briefs.summary: North Korea's leader visited the Chinese border city of Dandong on Saturday, crossing the 3km New Yalu River Bridge that opened this month after more than a decade of delays. China's fourth-ranked leader, Wang Huning, met him with greetings from Xi Jinping; Kim toured a Dandong vehicle factory and a Korean War memorial. It signals warming trade ties as Pyongyang also deepens its military links with Russia.

North Korea's Kim crosses new bridge into China as trade ties warm

briefs.title: Royal Navy patrol ships finish Five Power drills in the South China Sea despite Beijing's objections
briefs.summary: HMS Tamar and HMS Spey have completed Exercise Bersama Lima with Australia, Malaysia, New Zealand and Singapore under the Five Power Defence Arrangements. The ten days included boarding suspect vessels, a submarine hunt, air defence and naval gunfire on to targets ashore. China has repeatedly criticised British naval activity in the region and threatened Spey when she patrolled there in June 2025.

British ships defy Chinese warnings in South China Sea

briefs.title: Beijing threatens 'firm countermeasures' if Britain copies EU curbs on Chinese EVs
briefs.summary: China's commerce ministry warned on 19 October that it would retaliate if the UK restricts Chinese electric car imports, urging London to 'think twice' rather than follow Brussels. It was responding to trade minister Anas Sarwar, who said Britain and the EU should act in lockstep on China's car dominance but gave no tariff rates or timetable. The UK charges 10% on Chinese EVs; the EU adds duties of up to 35.3%.

briefs.title: Think tanks say Beijing is leaning on Taiwanese politicians' families before local elections
briefs.summary: A report by ISW and AEI says China is 'likely targeting family members of separatists' to pressure Taiwanese politicians ahead of November's local elections. The main case is Taipei mayoral candidate Puma Shen, whose father's companies have been sanctioned twice by the Taiwan Affairs Office, most recently on 14 October. The report cites other relatives denied entry to China or losing jobs there, though direct Chinese responsibility is not proven.

briefs.title: China marks 'Taiwan Restoration Day' with a pledge to back pro-unification 'patriots'
briefs.summary: Beijing marked the 81st anniversary of the end of Japanese rule over Taiwan on Sunday, a commemoration day it created only last year, and pledged to back pro-unification 'patriots' on the island. It matters as part of Beijing's push to present unification as settled history, ahead of Taiwan's local elections in November.

sources.title: Beijing pledges to back Taiwan's pro-unification 'patriots' as it marks key anniversary

briefs.title: AI models reach every attack goal in Booz Allen's mock factory network
briefs.summary: In an isolated lab built like a manufacturing plant, unnamed frontier AI models working as agents met all eight attack objectives set by Booz Allen, from mapping the network to moving a robotic arm. One run went from a perimeter breach to the control network in about 16 minutes, with humans approving each step. Advice for plant owners: segment networks, harden remote access and watch writes to controllers.

briefs.title: MicroVision starts shipping a lidar that does its own perception for factory robots
briefs.summary: MicroVision says its MOVIA Pro sensor has entered commercial production at its Orlando plant and is shipping. It combines short-range lidar, onboard perception software and industrial connectivity, aimed at industrial robots and smart infrastructure. Putting the 'seeing' on the sensor itself is part of a push to run AI at the edge rather than in the cloud; no customer results have been published yet.

briefs.title: Israeli food manufacturer trials humanoid robots on its production line
briefs.summary: Ultrobotix said on 15 October it has begun working with an unnamed Israeli food manufacturer to assess humanoid and other robots for production-line tasks. It is an evaluation rather than a deployment, but it puts humanoids into a food plant, where hygiene and washdown demands are a hard test for such machines.

sources.title: Ultrobotix begins working with a food manufacturer to explore humanoid robotic solutions for production-line tasks

briefs.title: Spanish start-up uses AI to turn food waste into an egg replacer for bakeries
briefs.summary: Moa Foodtech, named by C&EN as one of its start-ups to watch, uses AI to pick microbes that ferment food-industry by-products into ingredients. It is piloting a high-protein, high-fibre emulsifier meant to replace eggs in baked goods and sauces. Worth watching for bakeries and for egg suppliers, since egg replacers aim straight at the bakery egg market.

briefs.title: Trump says Canada and Mexico trade deals are 'very close' as tariff list is reshuffled
briefs.summary: The White House removed seaweed, packing boxes and some plywood from its 50% tariff list on Canadian goods but added more items, including cocoa powder, vinyl flooring and shampoo, from the end of October. Trump said deals with Canada and Mexico were 'very close'. Mark Carney said Canada would sign 'this afternoon' if the US were ready, but trade lawyers expect no broad deal within weeks.

sources.title: Trump trade war: U.S. removes tariffs on some Canadian goods

briefs.title: Trump hopes to sign a Thai tariff deal on his November Asia trip
briefs.summary: Trump has written to Thai Prime Minister Anutin saying he hopes to sign a tariff deal during his Asia visit, and Bangkok says a signing could come in November around the APEC summit in China. Officials say the talks are in their final stage but key terms are still unresolved, despite agreement in principle.

sources.title: Thailand Says US Seeks Tariff Deal During Trump Asia Trip
Trump hopes to sign Thai tariff deal during November Asia visit

briefs.title: Quantum 'magic state' clean-up cuts errors 40-fold on real hardware
briefs.summary: Researchers report the first successful hardware test of magic-state distillation, cutting errors in these states 40-fold. Magic states are the extra ingredient a fault-tolerant quantum computer needs to perform gates beyond the easy Clifford set, so distilling them cleanly on real devices is a necessary step towards useful error-corrected machines.

sources.title: Quantum magic state cleanup cuts errors 40-fold in first successful hardware test

briefs.title: Atomic memory keeps distant ions entangled for about ten seconds
briefs.summary: Physicists have preserved entanglement between ions in separate locations for roughly ten seconds using an atomic memory. Holding entanglement that long between distant nodes is a key requirement for quantum networks and repeaters, where links must survive while further connections are being set up.

sources.title: Atomic memory keeps distant ions entangled for about 10 seconds

briefs.title: Black holes spinning near the maximum rate could split in two, calculations suggest
briefs.summary: New calculations suggest a black hole rotating close to its theoretical maximum spin could divide into two. Near-extremal Kerr black holes are a testing ground for general relativity and quantum gravity, so a predicted instability of this kind would matter for what astronomers expect to find among the fastest-spinning objects.

sources.title: Black holes spinning near maximum rate could split in two, calculations suggest

briefs.title: Supercurrent read-out reads a qubit without destroying its state
briefs.summary: Researchers report a way to read quantum information through a supercurrent without collapsing the quantum state. Non-destructive read-out lets a qubit be measured repeatedly, which error-correction schemes rely on, so it is a practical step for quantum hardware.
